content.thinking:
I'm piecing together the timeline: the monthly-spend-feature flag was enabled at 09:26, triggering ZeroDivisionError crashes in spend_summary.py from 09:26 to 09:34, then the flag was reverted at 09:33:20 — though the service didn't seem to recover right away, since the incident status persisted just seconds later at 09:33:28.

Looking at the evaluation logs, the flag provider still shows the service evaluating "monthly-spend-feature=on" through the 09:34 bucket despite the revert, suggesting cached or stale evaluations kept the broken code path active even after the flag was flipped off. This would explain why the fix seemed refuted at 09:35:40 and the flag had to be re-enabled.

Maybe the verdict was made too hastily too — T21 checked only 8 seconds after the revert and judged it still at incident level, then waited until 09:35:40. I'm also noticing this same flag revert was tried and refuted in an earlier incident, which suggests a recurring pattern where flipping this flag off doesn't actually help, possibly because the change never propagates to the service's evaluation layer.

Tracing the causal chain: shoppers' account pages were failing with errors spiking up to 41.5% around 09:33, caused by a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py line 47, which traces back to the monthly-spend-feature flag being switched on by an admin at 09:26.

I'm checking what the records rule out here — deploys read from change events don't show anything coming back in the window, and no earlier change or flag state seems to explain the issue, so I want to be careful about how I phrase what was ruled out versus what was simply absent from the record.

Checking the change events read across the day (T9, T29), no deploy shows up in that window, and the replicas were all running a single revision (T10, T33). So I can only say a deploy wasn't found in what was read — not that it's definitively ruled out — since I don't have an earlier healthy measurement with that same change already in place.

Looking at candidates C1/C2, I notice the refutation applies to the revert action, not the underlying claim: the record shows reverting the flag didn't bring the service back, even though the flag went on at 09:26 right when errors started climbing. The record takes priority wherever it conflicts with the inferred chain, so I need to check whether this actually contradicts the flag being the trigger or just means the revert itself failed for another reason.

For the root cause itself, I'm tracing it back to F1: the flagged logic divides a shopper's monthly total by their purchase count, and for someone with zero purchases this month that's a division by zero. That matches the log line referenced in G5309, and since there's no supporting S or D row behind it, this counts as resting on an unrun reading, and it does reach a genuine cause.

Now I'm looking at the revert timeline — Gce95 kept logging the flag as on through 09:34, even in the minute after the provider marked it off, and G5309's errors persist to that same minute. That lines up with the Mitigation Agent checking the service eight seconds after the revert, seeing it still appear on, judging the revert refuted, and switching the flag back on.

For contributing factors, I'm noting that no test exercised the flag-on path for a shopper with no purchases before it went to production, so I'd propose requiring tests on flag-on paths before enabling any flag. I'm also looking at the rollout data showing the flag jumped from a mixed 111/89 split to full 200 traffic within a single minute, meaning there was no gradual ramp.

I'm also flagging that no one was paged since the alert wasn't tied to on-call, which should have triggered a person to step in when the automated revert failed, so I'd propose routing HighErrorRate alerts to on-call paging. I'm also considering whether cached flag evaluation kept the old behavior active even after the provider was turned off, which would have prevented the revert from stopping the harm, though that's an inference from the logs rather than something directly confirmed.

I'm second-guessing whether this timing evidence is solid enough to count as a real contributing factor versus a process observation, given the gap between the provider switch and the logged evaluation. I also notice this same flag was involved in a prior incident that was refuted, which might point to a recurring pattern worth flagging.

For prevention actions, I'm proposing a pre-enable CI check requiring tests on flag-on code paths before production release, a gradual rollout approach with automatic halt on error spikes, and routing the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop directly to on-call paging — mapping each to the corresponding contributing factor.

I also want a mitigation step to investigate why io-shop kept evaluating the flag as on even after the provider marked it off, fixing the flag propagation bug, plus a process step having the Mitigation Agent verify via the flag-evaluation log that the revert actually took effect before declaring success.

For stopping the harm, the plan is to switch the flag off again and confirm in io-shop's flag-evaluation log that it reads off and that the ZeroDivisionError has stopped.

For what's still at risk, since the underlying division bug at line 47 remains unfixed, requests taking the flagged path could keep failing with the same error for shoppers in that specific scenario.

For root cause, with the feature flag on, account page requests hit the spend-summary calculation that divides total spend by purchase count — and for shoppers who've bought before but not this month, that count is zero, triggering the ZeroDivisionError. The code never had a guard for this empty case, and the bug simply stayed dormant while the flag was off.

For the plain-language framing, I want to stay cautious about stating the division-by-zero mechanism as fact rather than Argus's best hypothesis, so I'll keep the "likely" qualifier there. The symptom line should just note that account pages failed for shoppers. Then I'm thinking about how to credit Argus for correctly tracing the failures back to the feature switch-on by correlating it with the failing log line.

I also need to note that Code-Fix proposed a draft pull request with tests shortly after the alert, and that Argus first tried the safer option of reverting the flag before anything else — though I should avoid naming the PR number explicitly and just call it a draft pull request. The tricky part is the revert being marked a failure even though there's no evidence the service itself picked up the change, since its own logs still showed the feature flag as on a minute after the provider reported it as off.

I should also flag that memory recorded an earlier incident where reverting this same flag didn't work, and nobody paused to ask why before trying the same revert again — plus the fact that no one was paged deserves to be called out as its own finding.

For assumptions, I'm noting that the claim the revert never reached the service rests on minute-bucketed flag-evaluation logs rather than direct measurement, and that the characterization of which shoppers failed relies on Code-Fix's reading rather than confirmed data.

Now checking whether CF-1 gets addressed by AI-1 per the guidance that a fix should answer a fault its own tests cover rather than a missing pre-change check — I conclude AI-1 answers no contributing factor directly, which is acceptable. I'm also tracing the timing chain: step 3 (flag switched on by admin) and step 1 (error rate climbing from baseline to peak), citing the relevant evidence sources, and ruling out deploys as a cause for step 3 based on the deploy history plus the fact the flag was previously off and healthy.

I also want to note the flag evaluation split at 09:26 shifting to fully on by 09:27, and confirm CF-2's counterfactual holds since errors would have stayed confined to a small share otherwise. Time to write this up.

action_items.item: Add a release check that blocks switching a feature flag on in production until tests covering the code path it enables have passed, including the edge-case accounts that path handles.
Roll out io-shop feature flags to a small share of traffic first, and halt and revert the rollout automatically when the error rate rises.
Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to the on-call rota so that a person is paged.
Find out why io-shop kept evaluating monthly-spend-feature as on after the flag provider showed it off, and make flag changes reach the service promptly.
Make the Mitigation Agent wait until the service's own flag-evaluation log shows the new state before it judges a flag revert.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account pages failed. From {began}, account page requests failed, and the service's own account page error rate peaked at {errors_at_worst} against {errors_before} before.
The account page requests failed because they raised ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. These errors first appear in the minute the incident began, and none appear before it.

ruled_out.what: A deploy. No deploy came back among the production changes read over the day before the onset and the longer window read later. When read, every replica was running a single revision.

causal_chain.step: The code that raised the error ran because an admin switched the feature flag monthly-spend-feature on at {P1.1}. Before that, the service evaluated the flag as off and account pages rendered normally. In the minute of the switch, its evaluations were split between off and on. From the next minute on, every evaluation came back on.

Switching the flag on broke the page because, according to Code-Fix's reading, the flagged path divides the shopper's total for this month by the number of purchases they made this month. That number is zero for a shopper who has bought before but not this month. Nothing guards the empty case, so line {F1.1}, the line the logs name, raises the error.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Turning on a new monthly spending summary sent shoppers' account pages through code that likely divides by the number of things a shopper bought this month, so it fails for anyone who has bought nothing yet this month.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that exercised the code path monthly-spend-feature turns on, for a shopper with no purchases this month, before the flag was switched on in production. According to Code-Fix's reading, the failure stayed hidden until the flag was on.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The division by zero would have been caught before the flag reached shoppers, and the flag would not have been switched on with the fault in place.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag went from off to on for every evaluation within a minute. No staged rollout that halts on a rise in errors was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The failures would have been limited to a small share of account page requests, and the rollout could have stopped before every request was taking the failing path.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: Nobody was paged. The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was not linked to an on-call incident.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person could have stepped in when the flag revert was judged not to help and Argus had nothing further to try, which would have shortened the incident.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: The service still logged monthly-spend-feature as on in the minute after the flag provider showed it switched off. No check was seen that confirms a flag change has reached the service.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The revert could have taken the failing path out of use at the service and stopped the failures, rather than leaving the service at the incident's level.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

went_well: Argus formed its candidate {T13.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, tying the failures to the monthly-spend-feature switch-on and to the line the logs name.
Argus reverted the flag, a reversible action, {T19.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
Code-Fix opened a draft pull request with a proposed fix and tests {T39.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
went_wrong: The flag revert was judged not to help without the service ever being seen to pick it up. The service's own log still read monthly-spend-feature=on in the minute after the provider showed it off, and the first look at the service came only {T21.1 - T19.1} after the revert.
Argus's memory held an earlier incident in which reverting this same flag was refuted. The same revert was tried again without first asking why it had not helped that time.

input.root_cause: Switching on monthly-spend-feature sent account page requests down the monthly spend-summary path. There, according to Code-Fix's reading, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py divides the shopper's total for this month by the number of purchases they made this month. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month, that number is zero, so the division raises ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1} and the request fails. In the files Code-Fix read, nothing handles the empty month before the division, and the path only runs when the flag is on.
input.still_at_risk: Because monthly-spend-feature was switched back on and the division the logs name was still in place, account page requests on the flagged path could keep failing with ZeroDivisionError, likely for every shopper who has bought before but not this month.
input.stops_the_harm: Switch monthly-spend-feature off again. Confirm at io-shop that its flag-evaluation log reads monthly-spend-feature=off, that account page requests stop failing with ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, and that the error rate falls back towards {errors_before}.
